content: Meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS) is a condition in newborns that can lead to severe respiratory distress, often associated with high rates of illness and death. The syndrome is thought to involve chemical pneumonitis caused by bile, bile acids, and pancreatic secretions present in the meconium. Based on this understanding, it has been hypothesized that corticosteroids, due to their anti-inflammatory properties, might be beneficial in managing this condition. The purpose of this review was to evaluate whether steroid therapy reduces the morbidity and mortality associated with MAS without causing adverse effects. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including PREMEDLINE, MEDLINE (1966 to April 2003), CINAHL (from 1982), Current Contents (from 1998), The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL, Issue 1, 2003), and the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials. Additionally, references from previous reviews and abstracts from Pediatric Research (1993–2003) were examined. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials that compared steroid treatment to no steroid treatment in neonates with MAS. The quality of each trial was independently assessed by the authors, and data were extracted and analyzed using a fixed-effects model in RevMan 4.2. Results were reported as mean differences (MD), weighted mean differences (WMD), and relative risks (RR), all with 95% confidence intervals. Three RCTs were identified, but only two were included in the review: Wu (1999) with 50 participants and Yeh (1977) with 35 participants. The third trial, Davey (1995), was excluded due to insufficient information about its methodology and results. Meta-analysis of the included studies showed no significant reduction in mortality with steroid use (typical RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.20 to 4.58). However, there was a small but statistically significant increase in the duration of oxygen therapy required in the steroid group (WMD 30.0 hours, 95% CI 8.4 to 51.6). In the study by Wu (1999), no significant difference was observed in the duration of hospital stay (MD 0.00 days, 95% CI -3.09 to 3.09) or the duration of mechanical ventilation (MD -1.10 days, 95% CI -2.79 to 0.59). Yeh (1977) reported no significant difference in the incidence of air leaks (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.18 to 2.26). Neither study provided data on long-term outcomes. The authors concluded that there is currently insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of steroid therapy in managing MAS. A larger, well-designed randomized controlled trial is needed to assess the potential benefits and risks of this treatment approach.
